easy.heading: Just Waking Up With Some Dots
easy.body:
I started today with the easy puzzle and it felt just like a warm-up stretch. The biggest clue for me was that sum target of 10 at the bottom in cells [3,0] and [3,1]. Since our dominoes are fairly small, I knew I needed big numbers there. Looking at the list, I had a [5,0] and a [5,3]. Putting those fives next to each other made perfect sense for that sum. Since cell [3,1] was a 5 from the [5,3] domino, cell [3,0] had to be the other 5 from the [5,0] piece.

Then I looked at the long column on the right where four cells had to be equal at [0,2], [1,2], [2,2], and [3,2]. Since I used the [5,3] domino at the bottom, and one half was at [3,1], the other half, which is the 3, ended up in cell [3,2]. That meant the whole column had to be 3s. From there, the rest of the pieces like the [2,3] and [6,1] just fell right into place. The unequal region at the top left was easy to check at the end to make sure no numbers were repeating where they should not be. It was a nice, gentle start to the day.

medium.heading: Getting Into The Groove
medium.body:
The medium puzzle felt a bit more like a real brain teaser. I immediately spotted those single-cell regions at [0,3] and [3,3]. A sum of 4 in one cell and 3 in the other meant those spots were basically gifts. After filling those in, I looked at the sum of 16 in the top left corner. To get a sum that high with only three cells at [0,0], [0,1], and [1,0], you need some heavy hitters. I used the [6,6] domino there, putting one 6 in [0,0] and the other in [0,1]. That left cell [1,0] needing to be a 4 to finish the 16.

One spot that made me pause was the sum of 1 for cells [2,2] and [3,2]. Since we only use whole numbers, it had to be a 0 and a 1. I had the [0,2] domino and the [3,1] domino available, and moving them around helped me clear the bottom row. I placed the [3,1] domino so the 1 was in that sum region. The tricky part was making sure the sum of 5 in the middle and the sum of 6 at [2,1] and [3,1] all worked together. It took a little bit of shuffling, but once the [5,4] and [5,3] pieces were in their spots, everything clicked. It was a fun little dance of numbers.

hard.heading: The Ultimate Pips Challenge
hard.body:
Wow, the hard grid today was huge, but I found a great way in. I started by marking the empty cells at [0,0] and [1,8] so I would not try to put anything there. Then I looked for the smallest sums. The sum of 0 at [6,4] and [7,4] was a total giveaway. Both cells had to be 0. Similarly, the sum of 1 at [6,7] and [3,4] really helped narrow things down. Starting with these tiny numbers gave me anchors to build around.

The big tricky part was the huge unequal region in the middle spanning six cells from [4,3] to [5,5]. I had to be so careful not to repeat any numbers there. The equals constraint for cells [4,2], [5,1], [5,2], and [6,1] was my breakthrough moment. I realized those all had to be the same value to satisfy the dominoes I had left, like the [5,5] and [6,6]. I used the 1 from the [6,1] domino to fill those spots. I spent a good chunk of time double-checking that [1,6] and [2,6] added up to more than 9. Once I placed the [4,6] and [4,0] dominoes, the whole right side of the board finally cleared up. It was quite a workout for my morning coffee!

explanation.tips: Focus on the small sums like 0 or 1 first because they have very few options. Also, look for the single-cell regions since they tell you exactly what number goes there. If you get stuck, look at your list of dominoes and see which big numbers are left, as they usually have to go into the large sum regions to help reach those high targets.
explanation.learned: I noticed today that unequal regions are much easier to handle if you fill in the surrounding equals regions first. It limits your choices and saves you from a lot of erasing later on. I also realized that 0 is your best friend in this game because it makes sums so much easier to calculate. When you see a sum of 0, you know exactly what to do without even thinking twice.

faqs.question: How do you play the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You place dominoes on a grid so that the numbers match the rules of each region. Some regions require numbers to add up to a specific sum, some require them to be equal, and others require all numbers to be different.

faqs.question: What does the unequal region mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: In an unequal region, every single number inside that marked area must be different. You cannot have two of the same number in that specific shape.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for the hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Start with the smallest sum regions and any single-cell regions. These give you fixed numbers that help you figure out which dominoes can fit in the surrounding areas.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed vertically or horizontally in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can place the dominoes in either direction as long as they fit the grid and satisfy the region constraints.

faqs.question: What does an empty cell mean in the Pips grid?
faqs.answer: An empty cell is a space on the board where no domino half can be placed. You should treat it as a hole in the puzzle and work around it.
